title: Subvert Trust Controls: Code Signing Policy Modification
shortTitle: Subvert Trust Controls: Code Signing Policy Modification
summary: Rather than forging a signature, this sub-technique disables the rule that demands one. On Windows that means turning on test signing so drivers only need a test certificate, or relaxing the driver signature enforcement state; on macOS it means disabling System Integrity Protection, which protects system files and the signing rules that apply to them. Application control products that require signed dynamic link libraries or executables can be relaxed in the same way. The change is made with command line utilities, a registry edit, a boot configuration edit, or by starting the machine in a recovery or debugging mode, and some implementations require a restart or leave a visible watermark on the desktop. Because development and testing sometimes need the same settings, the detection challenge is intent. The reliable signals are the configuration edit itself, who or what made it, and the unsigned kernel driver or executable that loads next.

beginner.definition: Some systems are set to run only software that carries a valid signature. This sub-technique is when an attacker switches that rule off. After the change, software with no signature and no valid proof of origin can run freely on the machine.
beginner.whyItMatters: Signature rules are what stop unknown drivers and programs at the lowest level of the system. Once the rule is off, attackers can load code that reaches deep into the operating system. The setting can also survive restarts. Detecting the change is often the only early warning you get.
howItWorks: Windows and macOS can require valid signatures before certain drivers or programs may run.
These rules may be enforced by default or switched on later by administrators.
An attacker holding high privileges edits the setting that controls that rule.
Unsigned code now loads with no complaint at all from the operating system.
The attacker installs a driver or program that would otherwise have been blocked.
beginner.example: Imagine a club that admits members only if they show a stamped membership card. The door staff follow that rule all night. Then a manager changes the rule to say that anyone may enter, and the staff keep working as before. The door is not broken and no card is forged; the rule itself was rewritten, so anyone can walk in.
takeaways: Signature enforcement settings should be monitored as sensitive configuration.
Any unsigned driver or system component loading after that change is a red flag.
Where development needs relaxed signing, isolate it and log every use.

objectives: Explain what driver signature enforcement and System Integrity Protection are for.
Describe how the policies are disabled through configuration or special boot modes.
Explain how this sub-technique differs from using a stolen or fake certificate.
Identify the command, registry and boot artefacts that reveal a policy change.
Recommend approval and monitoring processes for legitimate signing policy changes.
